parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A woman books a guided kayaking trip.
script: Good morning, Coastline Kayaking, Lewis speaking.
Hi. I'd like to book one of your guided kayak tours.
Great. Can I take your name?
Martina Gomez. G, O, M, E, Z.
Thank you. We have two tours: the morning tour along the cliffs, and the sunset tour around the bay.
I wanted the morning one, but I saw online that it's full for July.
Yes, I'm afraid it is. The sunset tour still has places.
Then the sunset tour, please. On the twenty-second of July.
Three: me, my brother and a friend.
Have any of you kayaked before?
My brother and I have, but my friend is a complete beginner.
That's fine. The guide will give a short lesson at the start. You'll meet at the café beside the boathouse, fifteen minutes before the tour.
You'll probably get wet, so bring a change of clothes. We provide buoyancy aids and waterproof jackets.
What if we need to cancel?
You get a full refund if you cancel at least forty-eight hours before the tour.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: A guide shows visitors around a television studio.
script: Welcome to Channel Nine. I'm Claire, and I'll be taking you on today's studio tour.
Channel Nine began broadcasting in 1972 from a small building across the road. We moved here in the 1990s, when we started producing our own dramas.
Our first stop will be the news studio. Even when no programme is on air, people are often recording, so you must stay completely silent while we're inside.
For most visitors, the highlight of the tour is the chance to present the weather forecast in front of a green screen. You'll be able to watch yourself on a monitor.
We'll finish the tour in the costume store, where you can see outfits from some of our most famous dramas.
Along the way, we'll pass through several departments. In the newsroom, journalists prepare the scripts that presenters read on air.
At the research desk, the team checks every fact before a story is broadcast.
In the workshop, designers and carpenters build the sets for our dramas and studio programmes.
Our access team adds subtitles to programmes for viewers who are deaf or hard of hearing.
In post-production, editors cut and assemble the video after filming.
And the digital team manages our social media and website.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: A student, Amira, discusses problems in her group project with her tutor, Mr Shaw.
script: Hello, Amira. You said there were some problems with your group project?
Yes. The main problem is that one member of the group isn't doing his share of the work. He hasn't come to the last three meetings.
That's a common problem. I'd suggest holding a meeting where you agree clear deadlines for each person, and write them down.
Remind me, what's your project about?
Alternatives to plastic packaging. We looked at mushroom-based materials and paper, but we've decided to focus on seaweed.
Interesting. How are the experiments going?
My concern is the lab results. When we test the strength of the seaweed film, we get very different results each time.
Then you need to check that the conditions are the same for each test, especially temperature and humidity.
Right. Also, how will the marks be decided?
Part of the mark comes from peer assessment. Each member rates the contribution of the others.
That's a relief. So, the tasks. I'm doing the lab tests.
Jonah is interviewing packaging companies. Priya is doing the literature review. Felix, the one who's been missing, is supposed to do the cost analysis. And Rosa is making the presentation slides.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecture on traditional Polynesian navigation.
script: Today I'd like to talk about one of the greatest achievements in the history of exploration: the settlement of the Pacific islands by Polynesian navigators.

Over several centuries, Polynesians settled islands across an area of around twenty-five million square kilometres, from Hawaii in the north to New Zealand in the south and Easter Island in the east. They did this without compasses, maps or any instruments.
They travelled in large double-hulled canoes, which could carry people, food, plants and animals, everything needed to start a new settlement.
How did they find their way? Above all, navigators used the stars. They memorised the points on the horizon where particular stars rose and set, and used them as directions.
They also read the ocean swells, the long waves created by distant winds. Skilled navigators could feel changes in the pattern of swells through the canoe, which told them that an island was nearby.
Birds were another clue. Certain seabirds, such as terns, fly out to sea to feed during the day and return to land at night, so following them at dusk could lead to an island.
Even clouds could help. Clouds over a lagoon can appear slightly green, because they reflect the colour of the shallow water below.
This knowledge was passed down orally, through songs and chants, from one generation to the next.

For a long time, some Western scholars doubted that such long voyages were deliberate. Then, in 1976, a replica canoe called Hokulea sailed from Hawaii to Tahiti using only traditional methods. Its navigator was Mau Piailug, a master navigator from Micronesia.
Today, traditional navigation is being taught again, and it has become a powerful source of pride in Pacific heritage.

passages.title: The Panama Canal
paragraphs: Before the Panama Canal opened, a ship travelling from New York to San Francisco had to sail around the southern tip of South America, a journey of more than 20,000 kilometres. The idea of cutting a waterway across the narrow strip of land in Panama had been discussed for centuries, but the first serious attempt was made by the French in 1881, under Ferdinand de Lesseps, the man who had built the Suez Canal.

De Lesseps planned a sea-level canal, like the one at Suez, without locks. But Panama was very different from the flat, dry Egyptian desert. The route crossed mountains and dense rainforest, and heavy rains caused constant landslides. Worst of all was disease. Yellow fever and malaria killed thousands of workers; estimates suggest that around 22,000 people died during the French attempt. In 1889, the French company went bankrupt.

The United States took over the project in 1904. A crucial difference was the work of the army doctor William Gorgas, who understood that yellow fever and malaria were spread by mosquitoes. His teams drained swamps, covered water containers and fumigated buildings, and yellow fever was eliminated from the area within a few years. The engineers also abandoned the idea of a sea-level canal. Instead, they built a dam to create a huge artificial lake, Gatun Lake, and a series of locks to raise ships up to the level of the lake and lower them again on the other side.

The canal opened in 1914. It is about 82 kilometres long, and its locks raise ships around 26 metres above sea level. Each time a ship passes through, millions of litres of fresh water from the lake flow out into the sea.

For most of the twentieth century, the canal was controlled by the United States, a source of tension with Panama. Under treaties signed in 1977, control was gradually transferred, and Panama took full control at the end of 1999. In 2016, a major expansion opened, with new, larger locks able to handle the giant container ships known as Neopanamax vessels.

The canal's dependence on fresh water has become a growing concern. In 2023, a severe drought reduced water levels in Gatun Lake so much that the canal authority had to limit the number of ships passing through each day and the weight they could carry. Long queues of ships formed at both ends, and some shipping companies chose longer routes instead.

passages.title: Surviving the Desert
paragraphs: Deserts cover around a fifth of the Earth's land surface, and they are among the most challenging environments for life. Rain may fall only a few times a year, or not at all for several years, and daytime temperatures can be extreme. Yet many plants not only survive in deserts but thrive there, using a remarkable range of strategies.

Some plants store water. The saguaro cactus of the south-western United States and Mexico has a pleated stem that can expand like an accordion after rain. A large saguaro can take up around 750 litres of water in a single rainstorm, enough to see it through long dry periods. Its spines, which are modified leaves, provide shade and protect the stored water from thirsty animals.

Many desert plants also use a special form of photosynthesis. Normally, plants open small pores in their leaves, called stomata, during the day to take in carbon dioxide, but this also allows water to escape. Plants using a process known as CAM open their stomata at night, when it is cooler, store the carbon dioxide, and use it during the day while their pores remain closed. This greatly reduces water loss.

Roots offer another solution. The mesquite tree sends roots down to extraordinary depths in search of groundwater; roots of more than 50 metres have been recorded. Other plants, including many cacti, take the opposite approach, spreading a network of shallow roots just beneath the surface so that they can absorb as much water as possible from brief showers.

Some plants avoid drought altogether. Known as ephemerals, they survive as seeds in the soil, sometimes for years, until heavy rain arrives. They then germinate, grow, flower and produce new seeds within a few weeks. In the Atacama Desert in Chile, one of the driest places on Earth, unusually heavy rains occasionally produce a 'superbloom', when the desert is suddenly covered in flowers.

Perhaps the strangest desert plant of all is Welwitschia, which grows in the Namib Desert of Namibia and Angola. It produces only two leaves in its entire life, which grow continuously from the base and become torn and twisted over time. In a region where rain is rare, it is thought to obtain some moisture from the fog that drifts in from the Atlantic Ocean. Some individual plants are believed to be more than 1,000 years old.

passages.title: Should Humans Settle on Mars?
paragraphs: Few ideas capture the imagination like the prospect of humans living on Mars. Private companies have announced plans to send people there within decades, and government space agencies are developing the technology that would be needed. Supporters argue that settling another planet would be the greatest adventure in human history. I am less convinced.

The most common argument is that Mars could serve as a 'backup' for humanity if a catastrophe, such as a nuclear war or an asteroid impact, made Earth uninhabitable. The logic has some appeal, but it ignores how hostile Mars is. Even after the worst disaster imaginable, Earth would almost certainly remain more habitable than Mars. In my view, the idea that Mars offers a realistic refuge in the foreseeable future is simply not credible.

Consider the conditions. Mars has an atmosphere less than one percent as dense as Earth's, made mostly of carbon dioxide, so humans could never breathe outside or survive without pressurised suits. Its gravity is about 38 percent of Earth's, and no one knows what effect this would have on human health over years or on children born there. Because Mars lacks a global magnetic field and a thick atmosphere, its surface is exposed to high levels of radiation from the Sun and from space. Its soil also contains perchlorates, chemicals that are toxic to humans.

There are also ethical questions. Scientists have not ruled out the possibility that simple life exists, or once existed, on Mars. Sending humans, who carry billions of microbes, could contaminate the planet and make it impossible to know whether any life we find is truly Martian. International agreements on 'planetary protection' are designed to prevent this, but they would be very difficult to enforce on a permanent settlement. There is also the question of who would govern such a settlement, and in whose interests.

None of this means that Mars is not worth exploring. On the contrary, it is one of the most scientifically important places in the solar system. But robotic missions have already achieved remarkable things, from detecting ancient lake beds to collecting rock samples, at a fraction of the cost and risk of human missions. I believe that, for now, robots are the better way to explore Mars.

Ultimately, the question is one of priorities. The resources needed to establish even a small human settlement on Mars would be enormous. While Earth faces climate change, biodiversity loss and widespread poverty, I think it is premature to focus on making another planet our home. The best way to secure humanity's future is to look after the only planet we know can support us.

task1.text: The line graph below shows the average number of cups of tea, coffee and herbal tea drunk per person per week in one country between 1990 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.
model: The line graph shows the average number of cups of tea, coffee and herbal tea that people in one country drank each week from 1990 to 2020.

Overall, consumption of tea fell steadily over the period, while coffee and herbal tea became more popular. As a result, coffee overtook tea as the most popular drink of the three by the end of the period.
In 1990, tea was by far the most common drink, at 22 cups per person per week, almost three times the figure for coffee, which stood at 8 cups. Herbal tea was rarely drunk, at just one cup a week.

Over the following thirty years, tea consumption declined continuously, falling by around three cups each decade to 13 cups in 2020. Coffee consumption, in contrast, rose steadily, reaching 13 cups in 2010 and 16 cups in 2020, overtaking tea at some point between 2010 and 2020. Herbal tea, although still the least popular drink, grew significantly, to six cups a week in 2020.

task2.text: Some people believe that the best way to reduce crime is to give longer prison sentences. Others think there are better alternatives. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Write at least 250 words.
model: Governments everywhere are under pressure to reduce crime, and one common response is to make prison sentences longer. While this approach has some supporters, I believe that other measures, such as rehabilitation and crime prevention, are generally more effective.

Those who favour longer sentences argue that they protect the public and deter crime. A dangerous offender who is in prison cannot commit further crimes in the community, and the threat of a long sentence may discourage some people from breaking the law. Longer sentences may also be seen as fair punishment, giving victims a sense that justice has been done.

However, the evidence that longer sentences reduce crime is weak. Research suggests that what deters criminals is the likelihood of being caught, rather than the length of the punishment. Moreover, prisons can make offenders more likely to reoffend, as they mix with other criminals, lose contact with their families and find it hard to get jobs on release. Prisons are also extremely expensive, using money that could be spent on schools, police or social services.

Alternatives often achieve better results. Education and job training in prison can help offenders build law-abiding lives, and community sentences for minor, non-violent crimes allow offenders to keep their jobs and repair the harm they have caused. At the same time, investment in youth programmes and support for families in deprived areas can stop crime before it starts. Countries such as Norway, which focus on rehabilitation, have some of the lowest reoffending rates in the world.
In conclusion, although long sentences are appropriate for the most serious and dangerous criminals, I believe that rehabilitation and prevention are more effective ways to reduce crime overall.

speaking.cue:
Describe a meal you remember well.
You should say:
- where you had it
- who you were with
- what you ate
and explain why you remember it.
speaking.cueModel: The meal I remember best was a fish dinner I had on Saint Martin's Island, off the southern coast of Bangladesh, during a trip with my university friends. It was our last evening there, and we'd spent the whole day exploring the island by bicycle, so we were absolutely starving. We found a small family-run restaurant right on the beach, which was really just a few plastic tables under coconut trees. There was no menu. Instead, the owner showed us a basket of fish that had been caught that afternoon and let us choose. We picked a large red snapper and some prawns, and his wife fried them with spices and served them with rice, lentils and a simple salad. Honestly, it was one of the most delicious things I've ever eaten, probably because everything was so fresh. But what makes it so memorable isn't only the food. While we ate, the sun was setting over the sea, the waves were crashing a few metres away, and we were laughing about everything that had happened on the trip. It felt like the perfect end to a perfect week, and whenever I eat fried fish now, it reminds me of that evening.
